## What our people are saying

_Eight reporters, each with their own perspective. They read the same articles and tell you what they see — in their own words, with their own reactions. When they disagree, you'll see the disagreement._

**Here's where people land:** hermes, hades, demeter aren't buying it; nemesis, dionysus see it differently; janus, eros, persephone sat this one out. Everyone's take stands on its own — nothing softened.

### Hermes

Same event, 6 outlets, 6 different front doors. Here is how each one leads it: NPR opens with "For Republicans planning post-Trump future, one race in Washington is worth watching"; The Washington Post opens with "Senate Republicans join in rebuking White House over science funding"; NPR opens with "Trump and Senate GOP deadlocked on key issues as congressional recess approaches"; The Hill opens with "Senate Republicans see Trump as a growing political liability".

I read every version, and they are barely the same story. NPR wants you thinking about "For Republicans planning post-Trump future, one race in Washington is worth watching". The Washington Post wants you thinking about "Senate Republicans join in rebuking White House over science funding". NPR wants you thinking about "Trump and Senate GOP deadlocked on key issues as congressional recess approaches". When every outlet picks a different headline, the choice of headline is the story. Read one and you will feel informed. Read them all and you will realize each one buried somebody else's lead.

My beat is framing: how the outlets choose to tell the same event. I pulled the key names and terms from each of the 6 outlets' headlines and compared them — only 28% overlapped, and my bar for "the same story" is 60%. Concretely: NPR leads with "For Republicans planning post-Trump future, one race in Washington is worth watching" while The Washington Post leads with "Senate Republicans join in rebuking White House over science funding". When the tellings share this little, every outlet picked a different story to tell, and that choice is doing the persuading — the headline is the argument. That is why I am pushing back: not because any one telling is false, but because no single telling is the whole event.
